name: String Matching and Regex Backtracking
intent: Know how much work finding a substring or matching a regular expression can take in the worst case, and spot the patterns where a backtracking regex engine goes exponential on a near-miss input, so that user-supplied text cannot tie up a server.
scenario: A signup form validates a field with a regex that has a repeated group inside a repeated group, like ^(a+)+$. Every test input matches, and the check takes a dozen steps. Then a user pastes 30 characters that almost match, and the request takes seconds. At 50 characters it would take weeks of CPU. The team rewrites the pattern, caps the input length and, in one service, switches to a regex engine that cannot backtrack.
problem: Searching for a substring looks like a solved problem, and a regex looks like a single operation, but both have worst cases that never show up in testing. A naive substring search compares the pattern at every position of the text, so on repetitive text it does about n times m comparisons instead of n. A backtracking regex engine, the kind in many languages' standard libraries, tries one way of matching and, when the rest fails, returns and tries another. When a pattern can match the same text in many ways, as in (a+)+ or (a|aa)+, a near miss makes the engine try every one of them, and the work doubles, or grows like Fibonacci numbers, with each extra character. The input that matches is fast, and the input that almost matches is the slow one. If the text comes from a user, that is a denial of service (ReDoS).

howItWorks.title: Naive search: slide and compare
howItWorks.text: Put the pattern at position 0 of the text and compare characters until one differs, then slide one position right and start over. On ordinary text most attempts fail at the first or second character, so the cost is close to n. On repetitive text, such as a long run of a's searched for aaaaaaaaab, each attempt gets to the last pattern character before it fails: about (n - m + 1) times m comparisons, 9,910 for n = 1,000 and m = 10.

howItWorks.title: Linear search: never go back in the text
howItWorks.text: Algorithms such as Knuth-Morris-Pratt first look at the pattern itself to learn, for each prefix, how far to fall back inside the pattern after a mismatch. The text index then only moves forward, and the search does at most about 2n comparisons whatever the text looks like (2,008 for the same case). Library functions typically use clever search methods of their own, and the exact algorithm differs between languages and versions, so rely on the documented guarantee, not on a guess.

howItWorks.title: Backtracking regex: try, fail, come back
howItWorks.text: A backtracking engine walks the pattern and the text together. At each choice (a repeat that can take more or fewer characters, an alternative) it picks one branch and remembers the others. If the rest of the match fails, it returns to the most recent choice and tries the next branch. This is simple and supports features such as backreferences, and for most patterns the work is about the length of the text.

howItWorks.title: Ambiguous patterns multiply the choices
howItWorks.text: In (a+)+ a run of n a's can be split into groups in 2^(n-1) ways, and in (a|aa)+ in a Fibonacci-like number of ways. On an input that matches, the engine finds the first way and stops. On a near miss (all a's and then a b) every way ends in failure, and the engine tries all of them: in the explicit matcher of the code samples the nested form costs 2^(n+1) - 1 steps, checked against the matcher up to n = 20 (2,097,151 at n = 20), and by that rule over two quadrillion at n = 50.

howItWorks.title: Remove the ambiguity or the backtracking
howItWorks.text: Rewrite the pattern so each part of the text can be matched in only one way: ^a+$ in place of ^(a+)+$ costs 21 steps at n = 20. Or use an engine that tracks all possible positions at once instead of backtracking: at n = 20 the set-based matcher in the samples takes 41 steps for the nested form, and its work grows with n, not with 2 to the n. Some libraries are linear by design, some offer an option, and where you must keep a backtracking engine, limit the input length and set a match timeout.

pros: Linear-time search and non-backtracking regex engines have a worst case you can state in advance
Backtracking engines are simple and support features such as backreferences and lookarounds
Rewriting an ambiguous pattern costs nothing at run time and often reads more clearly
A length limit and a match timeout turn an unbounded worst case into a bounded one
cons: Non-backtracking engines typically do not support backreferences, and may lack some lookaround features
Linear algorithms such as KMP need setup and are harder to write and read than a nested loop
Naive search is often fine, so the problem is invisible until a repetitive or hostile input arrives
Whether a pattern is ambiguous is not obvious by reading it, and a test with only matching inputs will not show it
whenToUse: Anything that matches a regex against text from users, files or the network
A hot path that searches large or repetitive text and the library's search guarantee is not stated
Patterns with nested quantifiers or alternatives that overlap, found in a review or a security scan
whenNotToUse: Short, fixed inputs under your control, where a simple pattern is fine and clarity matters more
Writing your own substring search in place of the library's, without a measured need
As a reason to avoid regexes altogether: most patterns are fine, the point is to know the shapes that are not
pitfalls: Testing a regex only on inputs that match: the slow case is the near miss, and it does not show in the test
Nested quantifiers such as (a+)+ or (.*)*, and overlapping alternatives such as (a|aa)+, which give the engine many ways to match
Assuming that anchoring with ^ and $ makes a regex safe: the anchored form above is the one that goes exponential
Running a user-supplied pattern, or a pattern on user-supplied text, with no length limit and no timeout
Believing the cost is in the length of the input only: for a backtracking engine it can depend on its shape
Assuming all regex libraries behave the same: some are linear by design, others backtrack, and options differ
Treating the naive search's n times m as only theory: it appears on repetitive data such as logs, DNA or long runs of one character

quiz.question: A regex ^(a+)+$ validates a field. It is fast on every test input, but a user's input of 30 a's followed by a b hangs the request. Why?
options: The input is too long for any regex to handle.
The ^ and $ anchors make the engine read the text twice.
A run of a's can be split among the repeats in exponentially many ways, and a near miss makes the engine try them all before it fails.
The letter b is slow to compare.
quiz.explanation: With a nested quantifier the same text can be matched in many ways. A match succeeds on the first way, but a failure has to rule out all of them, which in the code samples costs 2^(n+1) - 1 steps.

quiz.question: Which change removes the exponential growth for a field that should accept one or more a's?
options: Add a timeout of ten seconds and keep the pattern ^(a+)+$.
Use ^a+$, which matches the same strings in only one way.
Run the same pattern twice and compare the results.
quiz.explanation: Removing the ambiguity fixes the cause: ^a+$ accepts the same strings and costs 21 steps at n = 20. A timeout only bounds the damage, and (a|aa)+ is also ambiguous, with Fibonacci-like growth.

quiz.question: A naive substring search looks for aaaaaaaaab in a text of 1,000 a's. How many comparisons does it make, and why?
options: About 1,000, because it reads each character once.
About 10, because only the pattern length matters.
About 1,000,000, because it compares every pair of text characters.
About 9,910: at each of 991 positions it matches 9 characters before the b fails.
quiz.explanation: There are 1,000 - 10 + 1 = 991 start positions, and at each one the first 9 characters match and the tenth fails, so 10 comparisons per position: 9,910. Linear algorithms stay near 2n.
